title: Multiple Assignment
summary: Declare several variables at once, chain assignments, and swap values the Java way.
intro: Java lets you declare several variables in one statement and give several variables the same value in one line. It has no tuple unpacking, so swapping takes a temp variable. This lesson shows all three.

steps.title: Several variables in one declaration
steps.body:
Separate names with commas to declare several variables of the same type in one statement. Each name can have its own value.

```java
int a = 1, b = 2, c = 3;
double price = 9.5, tax = 0.8;
```

The type is written once and applies to every name, so one statement holds one type. To mix an `int` and a `String`, write two statements. The comma form needs a real type name: `var x = 1, y = 2;` is a compile error, because `var` allows only one variable per statement.

You can also declare first and assign later. Watch out: an initializer belongs to one name only.

```java
int a, b = 0;   // only b is 0, a has no value yet
a = 5;          // now a has a value
```

Java refuses to compile code that reads a variable before it gets a value. `System.out.println(a);` right after `int a;` is a compile error (*variable a might not have been initialized*), which catches the bug before the program ever runs.

Most style guides still write one variable per line outside `for` loop headers, because each line is easier to read, comment, and change. Use the comma form for short groups of closely related values.

example.title: Coordinates and size
example.prompt: Declare x, y, and z in one int statement and width and height in one double statement, then print each value on its own line.
example.explanation: The first statement creates three `int` variables but only gives values to `x` and `y`. The next line assigns `z`, so it is safe to print. The `double` statement needs its own line because it is a different type. `2.0` prints with its `.0` because it is a `double`.

practice.title: Color and name
practice.prompt:
Store a color and a name using two multi-variable declarations.

1. Declare `red` as 255, `green` as 128, and `blue` with no value in one `int` statement.
2. On the next line, assign 64 to `blue`.
3. Declare `first` as `"Ada"` and `last` as `"Lovelace"` in one `String` statement.
4. Print `red`, `green`, `blue`, `first`, and `last`, one per line.

Expected output:

```text
255
128
64
Ada
Lovelace
```
hints: Write the type once, then list the names separated by commas. A name with no `=` gets no value yet.
The `String` names need a second statement because they are a different type.

steps.title: Chained assignment
steps.body:
To give several existing variables the same value, chain the assignments.

```java
int a, b, c;
a = b = c = 0;
```

This works because an assignment is also an expression: `c = 0` stores 0 in `c` and then evaluates to 0. Assignment groups right to left, so Java reads the line as `a = (b = (c = 0));`. First `c` gets 0, then `b` gets the result of that, then `a`.

Each variable still holds its own copy of the value. Changing one later does not touch the others:

```java
b = 7;   // a and c are still 0
```

Every name in the chain must already be declared. `int a = b = 0;` does not compile unless `b` exists. Keep chains for simple resets to one literal. Beyond that, separate lines read better.

example.title: Reset the counters
example.prompt: Reset three fruit counters to 0 with one chained assignment and print them on labeled lines.
example.explanation: The counters start at different values. `apples = pears = plums = 0;` assigns `plums` first, then `pears`, then `apples`, so all three end at 0. Each label prints with `print`, which stays on the line, and the value follows with `println`.

practice.title: Starting scores
practice.prompt:
Give three players the same starting score, then change one.

1. Set `alice`, `bob`, and `cara` to 100 with one chained assignment.
2. Change `bob` to 85 on the next line.
3. Print each score on a labeled line: `Alice: `, `Bob: `, `Cara: `.

Expected output:

```text
Alice: 100
Bob: 85
Cara: 100
```
hints: Write the three names with `=` between them, then `= 100;` at the end.
Print the label with `System.out.print("Bob: ");` and the value with `System.out.println(bob);`.

steps.title: Swapping without tuples
steps.body:
Some languages swap with `a, b = b, a` or `[a, b] = [b, a]`. Java has no tuple unpacking or destructuring. Every variable has one declared type and an assignment stores a single value, so there is nothing to unpack. Swap with a temporary variable instead:

```java
int temp = a;
a = b;
b = temp;
```

The temp is required. Without it, the first assignment overwrites a value you still need:

```java
a = b;   // the old a is gone
b = a;   // b gets the new a, so both hold the old b
```

The same idea moves any number of values: save the one that gets overwritten first, shift the others, then put the saved one back. Give the temp the same type as the values and declare it right where you use it.

example.title: Swap two numbers
example.prompt: Swap two ints with a temp variable and print them on labeled lines before and after.
example.output:
Before
left = 5
right = 9
After
left = 9
right = 5
example.explanation: `temp` keeps the original `left` (5). Then `left` takes `right` (9), and `right` takes the saved 5 from `temp`. Three assignments, and no value is lost.

practice.title: Rotate three directions
practice.prompt:
Rotate three String variables one place to the left.

1. Declare one `String` variable named `temp` where the TODO is.
2. Rotate the values so `a` gets the old `b`, `b` gets the old `c`, and `c` gets the old `a`.
3. Keep the before and after printing that the starter already has.

Expected output:

```text
Before
a = north
b = east
c = south
After
a = east
b = south
c = north
```

tests.output:
Before
a = north
b = east
c = south
After
a = east
b = south
c = north

hints: Ask which variable gets overwritten first. That is the value to save in `temp`.
Shift in order: `a` must copy `b` before `b` changes, and `b` must copy `c` before `c` changes.
By the last step, the old `a` lives only in `temp`.

recap:
- `int a = 1, b = 2, c = 3;` declares several variables of one type. `var` cannot use the comma form.
- In `int a, b = 0;` only `b` gets a value. Reading `a` before assigning it is a compile error.
- Outside `for` headers, most code declares one variable per line.
- `a = b = c = 0;` assigns right to left because an assignment evaluates to the assigned value.
- Java has no tuple unpacking. Swap or rotate values with a temp variable.
